quests.sentence: Although it was raining we decided to go for a walk
quests.correctAnswer: Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
quests.hint: This sentence opens with a full clause of its own - subject and verb included - before the main idea starts.
quests.explanation: An introductory dependent clause, even a full clause with its own subject and verb, is followed by a comma before the main clause.

quests.sentence: Because the roads were icy the school closed early
quests.correctAnswer: Because the roads were icy, the school closed early.
quests.hint: This clause explains a reason and could not stand as a complete sentence on its own.
quests.explanation: A dependent clause beginning with 'because' takes a comma when it opens the sentence.

quests.sentence: When the alarm went off everyone rushed outside
quests.correctAnswer: When the alarm went off, everyone rushed outside.
quests.hint: This clause sets the timing for the main event and can't stand alone as a full sentence.
quests.explanation: An introductory time clause beginning with 'when' is followed by a comma before the independent clause.

quests.sentence: We decided to go for a walk although it was raining
quests.correctAnswer: We decided to go for a walk although it was raining.
quests.hint: This time the same kind of clause comes after the main idea instead of before it.
quests.explanation: When a dependent clause comes after the main clause, it usually needs no comma before it.

quests.sentence: The school closed early because the roads were icy
quests.correctAnswer: The school closed early because the roads were icy.
quests.hint: Compare this to the version where the reason came first - does the comma rule change when the order flips?
quests.explanation: A dependent clause following the main clause typically isn't set off with a comma, unlike when it opens the sentence.

quests.sentence: Everyone rushed outside when the alarm went off
quests.correctAnswer: Everyone rushed outside when the alarm went off.
quests.hint: Notice that reversing the clause order changes whether a comma belongs here at all.
quests.explanation: Since the dependent clause now follows the main clause, no comma is needed before it.

quests.sentence: If you finish your homework you can watch television
quests.correctAnswer: If you finish your homework, you can watch television.
quests.hint: This condition clause opens the sentence, setting up what needs to happen first.
quests.explanation: An introductory conditional clause beginning with 'if' takes a comma before the main clause.

quests.sentence: You can watch television if you finish your homework
quests.correctAnswer: You can watch television if you finish your homework.
quests.hint: The same condition now comes after the main idea - check whether the comma rule still applies.
quests.explanation: Since the conditional clause now follows the main clause, no comma is needed before it.

quests.sentence: Since the meeting ran long we skipped our break
quests.correctAnswer: Since the meeting ran long, we skipped our break.
quests.hint: This reason clause opens the sentence and needs its usual introductory comma.
quests.explanation: A dependent clause beginning with 'since' at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.

quests.sentence: My brother a doctor works long hours
quests.correctAnswer: My brother, a doctor, works long hours.
quests.hint: The phrase in the middle renames the subject and could be removed without losing the main point.
quests.explanation: An appositive that renames a noun, like 'a doctor,' is set off with commas on both sides.

quests.sentence: Our neighbor a retired teacher volunteers at the library
quests.correctAnswer: Our neighbor, a retired teacher, volunteers at the library.
quests.hint: Try removing the phrase in the middle - does the sentence still make complete sense?
quests.explanation: The appositive 'a retired teacher' adds extra information about the subject and is enclosed in commas.

quests.sentence: This restaurant a local favorite is always busy on weekends
quests.correctAnswer: This restaurant, a local favorite, is always busy on weekends.
quests.hint: The middle phrase gives extra detail about the subject without changing the main sentence.
quests.explanation: Since 'a local favorite' simply adds nonessential detail, it's set off with commas on both sides.

quests.sentence: The museum which just reopened last month has a new exhibit
quests.correctAnswer: The museum, which just reopened last month, has a new exhibit.
quests.hint: This clause adds extra detail about the museum but isn't needed to identify which museum is meant.
quests.explanation: A nonessential clause beginning with 'which' is set off with commas because it can be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning.

quests.sentence: My car which is fifteen years old still runs perfectly
quests.correctAnswer: My car, which is fifteen years old, still runs perfectly.
quests.hint: The information in the middle is interesting but not necessary to know which car is meant.
quests.explanation: Since there is only one car being discussed, the 'which' clause is extra detail and needs commas around it.

quests.sentence: The bakery which opened last spring sells amazing croissants
quests.correctAnswer: The bakery, which opened last spring, sells amazing croissants.
quests.hint: Test whether removing the middle clause changes which bakery is being talked about.
quests.explanation: Because the clause only adds background detail rather than identifying the bakery, it is set off with commas.

quests.sentence: The book that I borrowed from you was overdue
quests.correctAnswer: The book that I borrowed from you was overdue.
quests.hint: This clause is essential - it tells us exactly which book is meant, out of possibly many.
quests.explanation: A restrictive clause beginning with 'that' identifies which specific thing is meant and takes no commas.

quests.sentence: The employee that finishes first will get a bonus
quests.correctAnswer: The employee that finishes first will get a bonus.
quests.hint: Without this clause, we wouldn't know which employee is being talked about - that makes it essential.
quests.explanation: Since the clause is necessary to identify which employee is meant, no commas are used.

quests.sentence: The recipe that my grandmother gave me always turns out perfectly
quests.correctAnswer: The recipe that my grandmother gave me always turns out perfectly.
quests.hint: This clause narrows down exactly which recipe is meant, out of many possible recipes.
quests.explanation: Because the clause is essential to identifying the specific recipe, it takes no commas.

quests.sentence: The laptop that crashed yesterday needs to be repaired
quests.correctAnswer: The laptop that crashed yesterday needs to be repaired.
quests.hint: This clause tells us exactly which laptop out of possibly several - that's essential information.
quests.explanation: Since the clause identifies which specific laptop is meant, it is restrictive and takes no commas.

quests.sentence: My laptop which crashed yesterday needs to be repaired
quests.correctAnswer: My laptop, which crashed yesterday, needs to be repaired.
quests.hint: Since there's only one laptop being discussed here, this extra detail isn't needed to identify it.
quests.explanation: Because the speaker has only one laptop, the 'which' clause is nonessential and is set off with commas.

quests.sentence: The house that has the blue door belongs to my aunt
quests.correctAnswer: The house that has the blue door belongs to my aunt.
quests.hint: Out of several houses, this clause narrows down exactly which one is meant.
quests.explanation: The clause is essential for identifying the specific house, so it stays restrictive with no commas.

quests.sentence: The report for example includes last quarters sales figures
quests.correctAnswer: The report, for example, includes last quarter's sales figures.
quests.hint: This phrase adds a clarifying aside in the middle of the sentence, and a nearby word needs a possessive apostrophe.
quests.explanation: The parenthetical phrase 'for example' is set off with commas, and 'quarter's' needs an apostrophe to show possession.

quests.sentence: The results in other words were better than expected
quests.correctAnswer: The results, in other words, were better than expected.
quests.hint: This clarifying phrase interrupts the sentence and could be removed without losing the main point.
quests.explanation: A parenthetical phrase like 'in other words' is enclosed in commas because it adds a side note rather than essential information.

quests.sentence: The new policy of course still needs approval from the board
quests.correctAnswer: The new policy, of course, still needs approval from the board.
quests.hint: This aside adds the writer's attitude without changing what the sentence is actually about.
quests.explanation: The parenthetical phrase 'of course' interrupts the main sentence and is set off with commas on both sides.

quests.sentence: My cousin a nurse works nights weekends and holidays
quests.correctAnswer: My cousin, a nurse, works nights, weekends, and holidays.
quests.hint: This sentence has both an appositive and a list of three items - punctuate each part.
quests.explanation: The appositive 'a nurse' is set off with commas, and the three listed shifts are separated by commas as well.

quests.sentence: The hotel which we booked last minute wasnt as nice as the pictures
quests.correctAnswer: The hotel, which we booked last minute, wasn't as nice as the pictures.
quests.hint: This sentence has a nonessential clause and a contraction that both need attention.
quests.explanation: The nonessential clause 'which we booked last minute' is set off with commas, and 'wasn't' needs its apostrophe.

quests.sentence: Because the flight was delayed we missed our connection and had to rebook
quests.correctAnswer: Because the flight was delayed, we missed our connection and had to rebook.
quests.hint: This sentence opens with a dependent clause and also contains a compound predicate - check whether both need commas.
quests.explanation: The introductory dependent clause takes a comma, but since 'we' is the only subject performing both later actions, no comma is needed before 'and.'

quests.sentence: My uncle who taught me to fish still goes every weekend
quests.correctAnswer: My uncle, who taught me to fish, still goes every weekend.
quests.hint: Since the speaker has only one uncle, this identifying clause becomes extra, nonessential detail.
quests.explanation: Because there's only one uncle being discussed, the 'who' clause is nonessential and set off with commas.

quests.sentence: The employee who arrives earliest gets the best parking spot
quests.correctAnswer: The employee who arrives earliest gets the best parking spot.
quests.hint: This clause is necessary to identify exactly which employee is meant, out of many.
quests.explanation: Since the clause identifies which specific employee is meant, it's restrictive and takes no commas.

quests.sentence: Although were running late we still stopped for the dogs favorite treat
quests.correctAnswer: Although we're running late, we still stopped for the dog's favorite treat.
quests.hint: This sentence needs an introductory comma, a contraction fix, and a possessive apostrophe.
quests.explanation: The introductory dependent clause takes a comma, 'we're' needs its apostrophe for 'we are,' and 'dog's' shows singular possession of the treat.
